title: 9.5 Small Group · Group 1
contentObjective: With my small group, I can plot ordered pairs in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane — one step at a time, with support.
languageObjective: I can talk through each step out loud using a sentence frame and the lesson's key words.

noticeAndWonder.context: A colorful eight-petaled flower design sits on a coordinate grid. An orange octagon is centered on the origin O, four maroon hexagon petals point straight up, down, left, and right along the axes, and four teal petals fill the space between them — exactly one teal petal in each of the four quadrants.

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Captain Vega's Four Clues
revealWordProblem.text: Captain Vega's expanded treasure map uses base camp at the origin (0, 0). Her four clues are at A(4, 3), B(-5, 2), C(-3, -4), and D(2, -5), where the x-coordinate is units east (+) or west (-) and the y-coordinate is units north (+) or south (-). Question: In which quadrant does each clue land, and how do the signs of its coordinates tell you that without plotting?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: A(4, 3) is in Quadrant I because both coordinates are positive (+, +) — east and north. B(-5, 2) is in Quadrant II because x is negative and y is positive (-, +) — west and north. C(-3, -4) is in Quadrant III because both are negative (-, -) — west and south. D(2, -5) is in Quadrant IV because x is positive and y is negative (+, -) — east and south.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — How do you plot points in all four quadrants?
conceptIntro.intro: The coordinate plane has four parts called quadrants. A negative coordinate means you move left (for x) or down (for y) from the origin instead of right or up. We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: The signs of (x, y) tell you the quadrant: (+,+) is I, (-,+) is II, (-,-) is III, (+,-) is IV.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I will plot (-3, -4). I start at the origin (0, 0).
The x is -3, which is negative, so I move 3 units to the LEFT.
The y is -4, which is negative, so I move 4 units DOWN. I place my dot.
Both coordinates are negative, so the point is in Quadrant III.

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: Now let's plot (-5, 2). The x is -5, so which way do we move? Left 5 units.
The y is 2, which is positive, so which way? Up 2 units.
Left and up lands us in which quadrant? Quadrant II.
Sentence frame — say it with me: "The multiples/steps I need are ___ , and the answer is ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — with support
lines: Try the practice problems below. The hint button is right there whenever you get stuck — use it, that's smart.
Remember the key idea: The signs of (x, y) tell you the quadrant: (+,+) is I, (-,+) is II, (-,-) is III, (+,-) is IV..

discourse.prompt: How do the signs of the x- and y-coordinates tell you which quadrant a point is in?
discourse.sentenceFrame: In Quadrant ___, the x-coordinate is ___ and the y-coordinate is ___. I know (-3, -4) is in Quadrant ___ because both coordinates are ___.

approaching.stem: In which quadrant is the point (-4, 5)?
approaching.explanation: The x-coordinate is negative (left) and the y-coordinate is positive (up). Left and up is Quadrant II.
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: Look at the signs: x = -4 is negative and y = 5 is positive.
Negative x means move LEFT; positive y means move UP. Ask which corner of the plane is left-and-up.
From the origin, slide left 4 and climb up 5. Quadrants count I, II, III, IV counterclockwise from top-right.

approaching.stem: A point has a positive x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate. Which quadrant is it in?
approaching.explanation: Positive x (right) and negative y (down) = Quadrant IV (bottom-right).
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: Positive x pushes you RIGHT; negative y drops you DOWN.
Find the corner that is right of the y-axis and below the x-axis. Quadrants I–IV go counterclockwise from top-right.
Try a sample point like (3, -2): go right 3, then down 2. See which corner of the grid that lands in.

approaching.stem: Which point is located on the x-axis?
approaching.explanation: A point is on the x-axis when its y-coordinate is 0. (4, 0) is on the x-axis.
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: A point ON the x-axis never moves up or down — its height is zero.
Check each pair's y-coordinate (the second number). On the x-axis, the y must be 0.
Test (4, 0): right 4, up 0 — do you ever leave the horizontal axis? Now compare with (0, 4).

approaching.title: approaching — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Name the quadrant for the point (-2, 5).

workedExample.label: Student thinking
workedExample.work: The x is -2, so I move 2 units DOWN. The y is 5, so I move 5 units to the RIGHT.

approaching.correctWork: The signs were matched to the wrong axis. A negative x moves LEFT (not down), and a positive y moves UP (not right). So move 2 units LEFT and 5 units UP. Left and up is Quadrant II, not Quadrant IV.
hints: Which coordinate controls left/right, and which controls up/down? The x is always the left/right move.
x is -2 (negative → left) and y is 5 (positive → up). Left and up land you in which quadrant?

approaching.label: Match each ordered pair to its quadrant.
approaching.hint: Try the first step of the solution process.
hints: Only the SIGNS matter: (+, +), (-, +), (-, -), and (+, -) each belong to one quadrant.
Use the sign map: I = (+, +), II = (-, +), III = (-, -), IV = (+, -). Read each pair's signs and look them up.
Start with (3, 4): both positive, so Quadrant I. Now read the signs of (-2, 5) and use the map.

onLevel.stem: Point A is at (-5, 3). If you move 8 units to the right, what are the new coordinates?
onLevel.explanation: Moving right means adding to the x-coordinate: -5 + 8 = 3. The y stays the same. New point: (3, 3).
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.
hints: Moving right changes ONLY the x-coordinate. The y-coordinate stays at 3.
Add the move to the x-value: take -5 and count up 8. Careful crossing zero — use a number line if it helps.
Start at -5 and count 8 steps right: -4, -3, -2, ... keep going all 8 steps. Then keep the y as 3.

onLevel.title: onLevel — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Name the quadrant for the point (6, -1).

workedExample.label: Student thinking
workedExample.work: I'll read the coordinates as (y, x), so I treat this like (-1, 6): the first number -1 is negative (left) and the second number 6 is positive (up).

onLevel.correctWork: The order was reversed. In an ordered pair (x, y), x ALWAYS comes first. Here x = 6 (positive → right) and y = -1 (negative → down). Right and down is Quadrant IV, not Quadrant II.
hints: In (6, -1), which number is the x-coordinate — the first or the second?
x = 6 (positive → right) and y = -1 (negative → down). Right and down land you in which quadrant?

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Ordered Pairs in All Four Quadrants is matching each sign to the wrong axis — for example, seeing (-2, 5) and thinking "the x is negative so I move DOWN, and the y is positive so I move RIGHT," which lands the point in Quadrant IV. But the x-coordinate always controls left/right, never up/down: negative x means LEFT (not down), and positive y means UP (not right). So (-2, 5) is actually left 2, up 5 — Quadrant II. Before you submit, check that you used the x-coordinate for left/right and the y-coordinate for up/down, and never swapped them.

optionalActivity.name: Four-Quadrant Battleship
optionalActivity.intro: Optional — one more together if the group is ready: Captain Vega's fleet is hidden across all four quadrants of the treasure map — call out the coordinates to land each shot!

diagram.title: City Map: Four-Quadrant Locations
diagram.caption: City Hall sits at the origin; read each point's signs to see its quadrant — Library (-,+) is II, School (+,+) is I, Park (+,-) is IV, Hospital (-,-) is III.

connect.scenario: A city uses a coordinate grid to map locations. City Hall is at the origin (0, 0). The library is at (-3, 4), the park is at (5, -2), the school is at (2, 3), and the hospital is at (-4, -1).
connect.promptQuestion: How do four-quadrant coordinates help a city map locations in every direction from the center?
connect.prompt: The library is in Quadrant ___ because its x is ___ and its y is ___. The park is in Quadrant ___ because ___. Four-quadrant coordinates help because ___.

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: A point has a negative x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate. Which quadrant is it in?
exitTicket.explanation: Quadrant III is where both x and y are negative. This means the point is left of the origin and below the origin.
choiceFeedback: Quadrant I has both positive — you need both negative.
Quadrant II has negative x but positive y — check the y sign.
Quadrant IV has positive x — you need x negative too.
hints: Negative x and negative y — think about which direction each sign pushes the point.
Negative x means LEFT of the y-axis; negative y means BELOW the x-axis. Find the region that is both.
Plot a sample like (-4, -5): left 4, down 5. Count quadrants counterclockwise from top-right to name it.

smallGroup.label: Extra Support
smallGroup.who: Pull 3–5 students who struggled on the formative check / exit ticket for this lesson.
moves: Open with the worked example (I Do) — think aloud, don't just show.
Do the We Do together; require every student to say the sentence frame.
Release to the practice problems; the hint ladder is the safety net.

Watch for the common mistake: A common mistake in Ordered Pairs in All Four Quadrants is matching each sign to the wrong axis — for example, seeing (-2, 5) and thinking "the x is negative so I move DOWN, and the y is positive so I move RIGHT," which lands the point in Quadrant IV. But the x-coordinate always controls left/right, never up/down: negative x means LEFT (not down), and positive y means UP (not right). So (-2, 5) is actually left 2, up 5 — Quadrant II. Before you submit, check that you used the x-coordinate for left/right and the y-coordinate for up/down, and never swapped them.
Close with the exit-ticket check — celebrate the growth.
